idiom_name: enum + free recursive functions, compiler-checked exhaustiveness
implementation_notes: The idiomatic Rust answer to operations over a stable structure is a closed enum plus one free function per operation whose match arms cover every variant: adding an operation is a new function, and adding a variant is a compile error (E0004) in every function that matched exhaustively, so coverage is checked without accept()/visit() plumbing or vtables. Rust's own compiler falls back to the trait-based visitor only where the node set cannot be one enum: rustc_ast::visit::Visitor and rustc_hir::intravisit::Visitor provide overridable hooks with default recursive walks, and syn generates a Visit trait for macro authors - they exist because the AST is huge, the traversal must be overridable, and extensions come from other crates. Choose the trait form when many operations share one traversal and the node set is open across crates; otherwise enum + match is smaller, faster (no vtable, no Box) and exhaustively checked.
pitfalls: A wildcard arm (other => ...) or a generic helper swallows new variants and gives up the compiler's help; keep matches exhaustive.
Recursive enums need indirection (Box/Rc) and deep trees can still overflow the stack; untrusted input needs an explicit worklist instead of recursion.
A generic traversal over a large enum monomorphises per operation, which can blow up compile times; take &dyn or split the walk when that happens.
Ownership ties the visitor to the tree: a walker that stores references borrows the whole structure, and one that clones can double memory on large inputs.

variants.name: Visitor trait with walk_* defaults (rustc / syn style)
variants.idiom_name: trait Visitor with per-node hooks and provided recursive walk functions
variants.implementation_notes: The classic structure survives in Rust as a trait with one method per node kind plus default implementations that recurse (walk_*), so an operation overrides only the hooks it needs and calls the walk to continue; the double dispatch becomes a match inside each walk function. It is justified when the node set is generated or deliberately open across crates (lints, proc macros, rustc itself), when the traversal policy must be overridable (skip nested items, control depth, custom orders), and when operations are contributed by other teams. The trade is that coverage depends on discipline rather than on the compiler: rustc's own guide requires destructuring every field without `..` so that a new field breaks the build, because a trait with default bodies compiles happily when a new node kind is never handled.
pitfalls: Default trait bodies make missing coverage undetectable: a visitor that never handles a new node kind still compiles, so require the hooks (or review the walk) when the operation must be total.
Overriding a visit method without calling the walk prunes the subtree silently - documented as intended in the rustc guides, and still the most common bug in third-party visitors.
Trait objects limit the trait to object-safe methods and add a vtable per call, while generics monomorphise every walk per visitor; both choices have real compile-time or run-time costs.
Lifetimes: a visitor borrowing the tree must not also mutate it, which is why rewriting visitors need a separate owned or arena-based design.
